short: Codd's 1970 idea: data as tables of values, linked by matching values, queried by describing the result.
a row, in Codd's words: one value for each column of a relation.
a column, in Codd's words: a named, typed slot that every row has.
the names and types of a relation's columns: its shape, without the rows.
every relational operation takes tables and returns a table, so an answer can be queried again.
a collection that allows duplicates. SQL tables are bags; Codd's relations are sets.
changing how data is stored (an index, a disk) without changing the queries that read it.
a namespace inside a database that holds tables and other objects. public is the default one.
a question written in SQL. the answer always comes back as a table.
describing the result you want and leaving the steps to the system. SQL works this way.
what postgres sends after each statement, like SELECT 4 or INSERT 0 1: the command and a row count.
postgres running as a single process with no server around it. it's how PGlite runs.
the book's recorded output for a code block. a run in your browser is compared with it.
postgres's terminal client. it sends SQL to a server and prints what comes back.
a psql command that starts with a backslash, like \d or \x. psql handles it; the server never sees it as typed.
psql's \x mode: one line per column, for rows too wide to read.
a five-character error code. the first two characters are the class, like 23 for broken constraints.
where in your statement postgres gave up, drawn as a caret (^) under that character.
the part of a postgres error that gives the facts of the case: which key, which row, which value.
the part of a postgres error that suggests a fix. it's a guess, and it can be wrong.
ISO/IEC 9075, the document that defines SQL. revised every few years; the latest is SQL:2023.
one database's version of SQL: the standard, plus its own extensions, minus what it skips.
